## Purpose

We want to know **how** we should be using the mean / median ratio for log-transformed dataset detection.


```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| echo: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 10,
  fig.height = 8,
  dev = c("ragg_png", "svg"),
  dpi = 600
)
```

```{r}
#| label: targets
targets::tar_source(c("./packages.R", "R"))
tar_load(se_mmr_combine)
```

## Initial Distribution of Values

OK, so what does the mean / median ratio (MMR) look like across all the datasets? We are going to cap the high end at 200 and low end at 0.2, because otherwise it's too long-tailed to visualize and work with.


```{r}
#| label: fig-mmr-all
#| fig-cap: Log(Mean/Median) for all datasets.
plot_mmr_all = se_mmr_combine |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log(mmr))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  labs(subtitle = "All Values")
plot_mmr_200 = se_mmr_combine |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(mmr, 0.2, 200)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log(mmr))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  labs(subtitle = "0.2 <= MMR <= 200")
plot_mmr_all | plot_mmr_200
```

```{r}
#| label: trim-mmr
mmr_200 = se_mmr_combine |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(mmr, 0.2, 200))
```

## Do We Need All Datasets?

From the plot in @fig-mmr-all, it looks like there is a nice peak right around an MMR value of 1.0 that we could try to distinguish the two distributions.
However, something we need to consider as well is the maximum abundances observed in the datasets, because anything **already log-transformed** has to be able to survive being exponentiated.
We've recorded the maximum abundances in each of these datasets where available.

@fig-abundance plots the MMR vs the maximum abundances, for all datasets, and then for datasets with $0.8 \le MMR \le 1.2$.
Given the max abundances are log10-scaled, this implies there are datasets with an MMR right around 1.0, with abundances in the $1\times10^{10}$.
If we try to exponentiate those values, we will end up with $\infty$ in our datasets.

```{r}
#| label: fig-abundance
#| fig-cap: Exploring the distribution of maximum abundances with MMR value.
plot_all_abundance = mmr_200 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log(mmr), y = log10(max))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(subtitle = "All Max Abundances", y = "Log10(Max-Abundance)")

plot_slice_abundance = plot_all_abundance +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = log(c(0.8, 1.2))) +
  labs(subtitle = "0.8 <= MMR <= 1.2")

plot_all_abundance | plot_slice_abundance
```

If we restrict ourselves to just those datasets in the region we **think** represent log-transformed, and plot the histogram of max abundances, hopefully we see the **majority** are under a reasonable cutoff, as shown in @fig-abundance-interesting (red line represents an observed value of 100, black is 1000).

The cutoff lines for a maximum abundance are important.
The maximum value that R will handle doing for an exponent in $2\times10^{exponent}$ is about 1000. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-abundance-interesting
#| fig-cap: Distribution of maximum abundance within the MMR range of 0.8 - 1.2.
plot_slice_max_histogram = mmr_200 |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(mmr, 0.8, 1.2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log10(max))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log10(100), color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log10(1000), color = "black") +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  labs(
    subtitle = "Max abundance for data with (0.8 <= MMR <= 1.2), Red Line = 100, Black = 1000",
    x = "Log10(Max-Abundance)"
  )
plot_slice_max_histogram
```

## MMR Distribution After Max Abundance Limit

So now we can look at the distribution of MMR values after applying a cutoff on the maximum observed abundance, @fig-mmr-abundance-cutoffs.
Based on this plot, I think we can justify taking a max abundance cutoff, then looking at the MMR value, and if it's in a range, do exponentiation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mmr-abundance-cutoffs
#| fig-cap: Distribution of MMR values after filtering for datasets with the maximum abundance <= 100 (top) or <= 1000 (bottom). Black lines indicate MMR values of 0.8 and 1.2, respectively.
#| fig-height: 12
plot_mmr_max100 = mmr_200 |>
  dplyr::filter(max <= 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log(mmr))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(0.8)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(1.2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 200) +
  labs(subtitle = "MMR for Max-Abundance <= 100")
plot_mmr_max1000 = mmr_200 |>
  dplyr::filter(max <= 1000) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log(mmr))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(0.8)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(1.2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 200) +
  labs(subtitle = "MMR for Max-Abundance <= 1000")
plot_mmr_max100 / plot_mmr_max1000
```

## Effect On Negative Abundances

```{r}
#| label: filter-neg
mmr_has_neg = mmr_200 |>
  dplyr::filter(N_neg >= 2)
perc_neg_interesting = (mmr_has_neg |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(mmr, 0.8, 1.2), max <= 1000) |>
  nrow() /
  nrow(mmr_has_neg))
out_neg_interesting = paste0(
  format(perc_neg_interesting * 100, digits = 2),
  "%"
)
```

This all started with discovering some log-transformed datasets existing in the datasets that still had negative values, so we should check how many of the datasets with negative values are represented in these subsets.
Although the scatterplot shows datasets all over that space (see @fig-negatives), `{r} out_neg_interesting` of the datasets are in the region where we consider the most likely for log-transformed datasets (max abundance <= 1000, 0.8 <= MMR <= 1.2).

```{r}
#| label: fig-negatives
#| fig-cap: MMR vs max-abundance for datasets with more than 2 negative values.
plot_mmr_neg_max = mmr_has_neg |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log(mmr), y = log10(max))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(1000)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    subtitle = "Datasets N-neg >= 2, Black = 1000",
    y = "Log10(Max-Abundance)"
  )
plot_mmr_neg_max
```

## Can We Put Some Confidence On A Distribution?

OK, so if we take that set, can we figure out the distribution, and be confident that we have it covered?
One way would be to pretend the data is normal-ish, and scale the MMR data, to have mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1, and then plot the histogram to see how many SD's we cover, as shown in @fig-distribution.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distribution
#| fig-cap: Histogram of scaled (mean = 0, SD = 1) MMR values (0.8 <= MMR <= 1.2, max-abundance <= 1000).
mmr_consider = mmr_200 |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(mmr, 0.8, 1.2), max <= 1000) |>
  dplyr::mutate(mmr_scale = scale(mmr))
mmr_consider |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mmr_scale)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  labs(subtitle = "Scaled MMR values (0.8 <= MMR <= 1.2)", x = "Scaled(MMR)")
```

## Conclusion

I think we can justify doing a max abundance cutoff <= 1000, and then consider mean-median-ratios between 0.8 and 1.2 as likely log-transformed.
